source: Wang, Petridis, Kwon, Ma, Chilton (2023) PopBlends: strategies for conceptual blending with large language models
finding: GPT-3 was used to find the connecting concept between a pop-culture domain and a product. Three ways to do it (no GPT, half GPT, full GPT) were about equally accurate for one answer, and nearly always gave at least one good answer in five.
numbers: Annotated 5 pop-culture domains x 6 products. Share of connecting concepts relevant to both domains: No-GPT 56.0%, Half-GPT 55.3%, Full-GPT 58.7% (overall 56.7%). At least one good concept among five: 90.0%, 96.6%, 93.3% (93.3% overall). Two raters, Cohen kappa 0.43 (moderate); a concept counted true if either rater said true.
limits: Rater agreement is only moderate and the lenient either-rater rule inflates scores. GPT-3 only, 2021-era model. Small topic set.
agent_relevance: A coded blend operator can ask for several candidate bridges and rely on the best of five, not on the first. Do not trust any single bridge: only about 56% are valid.

source: Wang, Petridis, Kwon, Ma, Chilton (2023) PopBlends: strategies for conceptual blending with large language models
finding: Full-GPT found connections the classic NLP route missed, but also made up connections: it claimed links that do not exist in the source material.
numbers: No numbers for the failure rate. Example given: GPT-3 claimed a toothbrush-cleaning link counts as a Star Wars link; it also invented plot events.
quote: GPT-3 may fail to make a connection to the pop culture domain, although it claims to.
limits: Qualitative; authors' own examples.
agent_relevance: Supports guardrails G2/G3: every claimed bridge needs a code check against a source, because the model asserts links it cannot support.

source: Wang, Petridis, Kwon, Ma, Chilton (2023) PopBlends: strategies for conceptual blending with large language models
finding: When GPT-3 acts as a knowledge base of character attributes, accuracy depends on the attribute type. Adjectives are reliable; catchphrases are not.
numbers: Relevant attributes per entity (out of 5): adjectives 3.93 (79%), activities 2.89 (58%), catchphrases 1.75 (35%), all 2.86 (57%); inter-rater kappa 0.41 overall (0.32 to 0.47). 200 collected entities were checked against Fandom wikis: 100% relevant, 4% (8 of 200) of marginal importance.
limits: Pop-culture entities only. Moderate rater agreement.
agent_relevance: In the extract-features-of-each-input step, prefer abstract trait lists over exact recall of facts; verify recalled facts.

source: Wang, Petridis, Kwon, Ma, Chilton (2023) PopBlends: strategies for conceptual blending with large language models
finding: Once a connecting concept is given, GPT-3 expands the product side into scenes almost perfectly, and the pop-culture side less well.
numbers: Product scenes judged related to the connecting concept: 98.3%. Raw relatedness: product scenes 80.0% vs pop-culture scenes 63.4%. Classic plot-sentence search for pop-culture scenes was more faithful than GPT-3 scenes.
limits: Two different measures appear in the same section; the 89.1% vs 75.9% pair in the text is not clearly labelled, so it is not used here.
agent_relevance: The model is strong when it elaborates a known bridge in a generic domain, weaker when it must recall exact facts about a specific fictional world. Use it for elaboration, use retrieval for facts.

source: Wang, Petridis, Kwon, Ma, Chilton (2023) PopBlends: strategies for conceptual blending with large language models
finding: In a within-subject study, people made more blend ideas with the tool than with web search, with less mental effort.
numbers: 10 participants, 6 blends each (3 baseline, 3 tool). Ideas per pair: 2.03 (SD 0.84) with PopBlends vs 0.87 (SD 0.56) with web search; paired Wilcoxon p < 0.001. NASA-TLX mental demand 2.85 (SD 1.08) vs 5.80 (SD 2.14), p = 0.004; effort also lower (p = 0.006).
limits: N = 10, university sample. Counts ideas, not idea quality or whether blends were better. Baseline was web search, not an LLM chat.
agent_relevance: Shows LLM-assisted candidate generation helps humans produce more blends. It does not show better final answers, so it is no proof for reasoning gains.

source: Lu et al. (2025) Misty: UI prototyping through interactive conceptual blending
finding: Misty blends a source UI with an example UI or a sketch by asking GPT-4o to rewrite code. It uses few-shot prompting with chain of thought, and treats code as the blending substrate so the result can be edited and re-run.
numbers: 14 frontend engineers, 103 logged blending operations. Operation mix: global blending 36 (34.95%), drag-and-drop 35 (33.98%), regenerate 19 (18.5%), semantic diff 9 (8.74%), code edit 4 (3.88%). Mean satisfaction per operation 3.2 of 5 (median 3, SD 1.3). Nine of 14 rated at least one output very satisfied.
limits: Usability study, no control arm, no accuracy measure. Satisfaction depends on expectations of visual detail and on random output variation.
agent_relevance: Design to copy: the blend is a code artefact that can be diffed, toggled and re-run, which fits our run-the-blend check. Satisfaction of about 3.2 shows blends are hit and miss, so selection needs a check.

source: Lu et al. (2025) Misty: UI prototyping through interactive conceptual blending
finding: Users valued serendipitous blends and wanted fine control. Many wanted to keep the good part of a blend and discard the rest (semantic-diff toggles).
numbers: Themes from interviews with 14 participants. Six participants (P2, P5, P7, P8, P10, P14) said they enjoyed surprising outputs; the paper also notes serendipity is a double-edged sword.
limits: Self-report. Frontend engineers only.
agent_relevance: A selective-projection step works best when each projected element can be switched on or off and the blend re-checked, not accepted whole.

source: Ge and Parikh (2021) Visual conceptual blending with large-scale language and vision models
finding: Masked language models can propose objects that share a property with an input (the shape of the moon is spherical, so shell). This beat a ConceptNet lookup at recovering the property that links two things in similes.
numbers: Simile dataset (Chakrabarty et al. 2020); 1000 candidates per method; precision at 10, 100, 1000. Precision with ConceptNet was significantly lower than with language models; larger language models were better. In the extracted table the best row reaches 66.38 at P@1000; one GPT-family row shows 53.08 and one BERT-large row 37.33 (row labels are scrambled in the PDF text, so assignment per model is uncertain). 96.34% of objects were found in ConceptNet; 688.9 relations returned on average when 1000 were asked.
limits: Short workshop paper. Property recovery in similes is a proxy for blending, not blending itself. Old models (BERT, GPT-2 class).
agent_relevance: Supports an ask-the-model-for-the-shared-property step (cross-space matching) over a fixed knowledge base. Candidate lists, not single answers.

source: Ge and Parikh (2021) Visual conceptual blending with large-scale language and vision models
finding: Image blends from text descriptions: CLIP-guided generators beat a plain GAN. Evaluation used Fauconnier and Turner's optimality principles as questions.
numbers: 20 blend descriptions (10 from the reasoning pipeline, 10 written by the authors); 3 generators compared pairwise; each question answered by 9 unique Mechanical Turk subjects; 6 questions (recognise object 1, recognise object 2, blend quality, description fit, interest, aesthetics). BigSleep and DeepDaze significantly beat DF-GAN; BigSleep preferred over DeepDaze. Exact percentages are only in a figure.
limits: Only 20 descriptions. The text read does not report whether model-written descriptions beat human-written ones.
agent_relevance: Gives a cheap rubric for scoring a blend: does it keep input 1, keep input 2, integrate, fit the description. Could become code checks or a blind judge.

source: Xu, Zhang, Gao, Deussen, Lee, Tang (2026) Beyond pixels: visual metaphor transfer via schema-driven agentic reasoning
finding: A multi-agent loop built on conceptual blending theory. It extracts a schema from a reference (subject, carrier, generic space, intent), a transfer agent keeps the generic space fixed while choosing a new carrier, and a diagnostic agent checks the output and backtracks through levels.
numbers: Schema is a 7-tuple whose parts map to blending components. Iteration threshold set to 5. Gemini-3-pro is both the VLM and LLM; Banana-pro makes the images. Tested on a 126-metaphor set.
limits: Preprint. The same model family acts as generator, critic and one of three judges, a self-preference risk the authors reduce with judges from other providers.
agent_relevance: Closest published match to our O7: input spaces, a generic space held invariant, selective projection, a critic that backtracks to a named level. A cap of 5 iterations is a ready design.

source: Xu, Zhang, Gao, Deussen, Lee, Tang (2026) Beyond pixels: visual metaphor transfer via schema-driven agentic reasoning
finding: Ablation by human raters: a single strong one-shot blending prompt helps a lot over a plain instruction, but the full staged pipeline beats it, and removing the diagnostic step costs the most among the agents.
numbers: 100 participants (age 14-55; 45 male, 55 female), 5-point scales, each rated 45 images per method. Means on five scales (MR, MI, VA, VI, VQ): Direct Prompt 3.62, 2.75, 2.96, 3.75, 3.65; Strong Prompt (one-shot blending prompt) 3.97, 3.69, 3.77, 3.89, 4.09; without blending description 3.88, 3.66, 3.68, 4.04, 4.12; without Transfer agent 4.01, 3.71, 3.83, 4.33, 4.25; without Diagnostic agent 4.26, 4.05, 3.98, 4.61, 4.48; full 4.47, 4.56, 4.51, 4.74, 4.76. Metaphor ingenuity (MI) rises from 2.75 (plain) to 3.69 (prompt alone) to 4.56 (full loop).
limits: Only the MR and MI scale names were confirmed in the text read; VA, VI, VQ are not labelled in the extract. Task is image metaphor, not reasoning. Table row alignment is from PDF text and may be imperfect.
agent_relevance: Evidence that a staged blend with a critic helps over one prompt. The biggest single jump is from a plain to a structured prompt, the next from adding the loop.

source: Xu, Zhang, Gao, Deussen, Lee, Tang (2026) Beyond pixels: visual metaphor transfer via schema-driven agentic reasoning
finding: Automatic VLM judges and head-to-head human preference favour the pipeline over frontier image generators.
numbers: Human pairwise: pipeline preferred over GPT-Image in 64.44%, Banana-pro 67.11%, Midjourney 72.89%, BAGEL 76.22% of pairs; judged inferior in fewer than 10% of pairs. Analogy appropriateness (AA) gain of 16.8% over the runner-up. Gemini-3-pro judge, metaphor consistency (MC): BAGEL 5.17, Midjourney 5.33, GPT-Image 8.08, Banana-pro 8.75, Direct Prompt 8.79, Strong Prompt 9.02. Judges from three providers (Gemini-3-pro, GPT-5.2, Claude-4.5) agreed the method led.
limits: VLM scores for the strong baselines are close together (8.08 to 9.02), so differences there are small. Judges overlap with the pipeline's own model.
agent_relevance: An LLM judge separates close options poorly; human or code checks matter more at the top end.

source: Schapiro et al. (2026, v6) Measuring combinatorial creativity in large language models and humans (KOMBINE)
finding: The largest LLM test of blending so far: 35 models, tasks of association, analogy and blending between random Wikidata entities. Blending is hardest, and the failure is finding a shared abstraction (generic space), not describing the blend.
numbers: Valid outputs averaged over 35 LLMs: association 59.0%, analogy 53.4%, blend 43.4%. Models are 10 to 16 percentage points better at association and analogy than blends. Given a valid generic space, a coherent blended concept followed 97.1% of the time (abstraction bottleneck). Exception noted: gpt-5.6-sol 64.8% on blending but 55.4% on analogy.
quote: even frontier LLMs struggle to find a shared abstraction between inputs and instantiate a coherent blended space
limits: Preprint, model names as printed. Judged by an LLM panel of 3, not by ground truth. Random entity pairs, not a goal-directed task.
agent_relevance: Tells us where to put the check: the generic-space step. A code check that the generic space truly fits both inputs is the highest-value gate in a blend operator.

source: Schapiro et al. (2026, v6) Measuring combinatorial creativity in large language models and humans (KOMBINE)
finding: Humans scored below almost every LLM on all three tasks, and also found blending hardest.
numbers: 75 human participants; skipped items scored zero. Humans vs LLMs: association 22.1% vs 59.0%, analogy 32.9% vs 53.4%, blend 12.8% vs 43.4%. For LLMs association is easier than analogy; for humans analogy is easier than association. Humans use more physical, everyday words; LLMs use more people, places and communication terms.
limits: Zero scoring for skipped items lowers human numbers. Online participants, unknown motivation. The same LLM judges scored both groups.
agent_relevance: Do not use humans-are-better-at-blending as a design premise. The weak point is validity, so the schema should verify.

source: Schapiro et al. (2026, v6) Measuring combinatorial creativity in large language models and humans (KOMBINE)
finding: Models reuse each other's blends (inventive homogeneity). This is far worse for blends than analogies and stronger within one provider.
numbers: One in five invented concepts (412 of 2,070, 19.9%) reuses properties another model invented. For blend-invented concepts reuse is 94.7% vs 36.3% for analogy; (>=2)-multiples 37.3% vs 2.6% (14.3x). Same provider vs different provider: 9.3% vs 4.1% (2.3x).
limits: Embedding-based overlap (all-MiniLM-L6-v2). Sampling at T=0.9, top-p/top-k off, default reasoning level.
agent_relevance: Supports G4: blends from one model are not independent. Sampling the same model many times will not give diverse blends; vary the inputs or retrieved material instead.

source: Schapiro et al. (2026, v6) Measuring combinatorial creativity in large language models and humans (KOMBINE)
finding: Reliability of the LLM judging panel is only fair, and agreement with humans is bounded.
numbers: Analogy and blend judges: Claude Haiku 4.5, gpt-o3, GPT-5.4 panel; fair-to-good reliability; they agree with human judgement 75% of the time on items where all three judges agree. Factuality judge: Claude Haiku 4.5.
limits: The 75% holds only for unanimous items, which are probably the easier ones.
agent_relevance: A model judge of is-this-a-valid-blend errs roughly 1 in 4 even when unanimous. Pair it with code checks.

source: Peng et al. (2025) Probing and inducing combinational creativity in vision-language models
finding: A three-level prompt (Identification, Explanation, Implication) based on blending theory: name the input spaces, extract the shared attributes, then derive the implication. Adding the explanation step gave better creative images than identification plus implication alone.
numbers: CreativeMashup: 666 artist-made visual mashups annotated by experts. Midjourney mean rank (lower is better) IEI 1.98 vs II (no explanation step) 2.40. Winning rate against human experts rose from 0.26 to 0.35 with IEI. Friedman test across the three conditions p <= 0.0001 for all models; Stable Diffusion 3 showed minimal gain.
limits: Rankings by human raters; win rates for other models only in a figure. Gain is larger for models that follow instructions better.
agent_relevance: Direct evidence that the middle blending step (extract shared attributes) is what helps, not just a longer prompt. Worth copying as the cross-space matching slot.

source: Peng et al. (2025) Probing and inducing combinational creativity in vision-language models
finding: Length control: the gain is not due to longer prompts.
numbers: Prompt length IEI mean 514.53 vs II 487.95 (t = -0.84, p = 0.404). In 46.0% of cases where IEI beat II, the IEI prompt was shorter.
limits: Length only; wording quality is not controlled.
agent_relevance: Useful template for our own scaffold tests: always check that the gain is not from extra text.

source: Peng et al. (2025) Probing and inducing combinational creativity in vision-language models
finding: Understanding blends in images: top models beat average people but not experts.
numbers: Identification: Gemini-1.5-Pro 73.67% precision, 81.33% recall; average humans 53.42% precision, 70.33% recall. Explanation: humans 69.89% precision, ranked third. Implication task win rate: human experts 78.3%, average participants 51%; GPT-4o and Claude-3.5-Sonnet beat average humans on all three tasks. Open-ended answers scored with GPT-4o as judge, which agreed with two human experts 85.1% and 81.6% on 200 comparisons.
limits: The text and a figure caption disagree on whether fusion or replacement mashups are easier (text: fusion, 9 of 11 models). Flagged, not resolved. Older models (GPT-4o, Claude-3.5).
agent_relevance: Understanding a given blend is easier than inventing a good one, so an agent may recognise a good blend better than it makes one: rank candidates by a check.

source: Peng et al. (2025) Probing and inducing combinational creativity in vision-language models
finding: The concept step is strong but the image step is the bottleneck.
numbers: GPT-4o concept-level combinations: 90% (36 of 40) of DALL-E 3 examples integrated the objects and conveyed the theme; 27.8% (10 of 36) of well-formed descriptions still failed to render satisfactorily.
limits: Small sample (40). Image-specific.
agent_relevance: For text-only agents, the concept step is cheaper to trust than the execution step. Always run the blend.

source: Hernandez et al. (2024) Alien recombination: exploring concept blends beyond human cognitive availability in visual art
finding: Raising sampling temperature gives new combinations but not combinations no artist would think of. Reaching those needed explicit search: two small GPT-2 models, one for artwork co-occurrence and one for what is cognitively available to artists, with ranking of sequences that fit but are unavailable.
numbers: Concept space from WikiArt via CLIP, nine features plus style, limited to WordNet Core. Above temperature 1, 85% of combinations contain at least one concept new at artwork level; at temperature 3, more than half of combinations have no cognitively unavailable concept (Ncog = 0). GPT-4 pairwise judging and ResNet152 embedding distance both rated alien-sampled images as more novel than baseline.
limits: Novelty judged by GPT-4 and embeddings, not by people; DALL-E output stays near the training distribution. Measures novelty, not truth or usefulness.
agent_relevance: Randomness (temperature) is not a substitute for search over unlike pairs. Choose the input pair by an explicit rule (for example low co-occurrence plus a fit score), not by sampling noise.

source: Matsuhira, Kastner, Komamizu, Hirayama, Ide (2024) Investigating conceptual blending of a diffusion model for improving nonword-to-image generation
finding: Stable Diffusion blends two prompts when their text embeddings are mixed, and blending peaks at the midpoint. Two measures: BCD (a true blended depiction) and MCD (both concepts present, not necessarily fused).
numbers: 1,000 image generations across nine interpolation ratios. At the midpoint (0.5): BCD 0.621, MCD 0.862. Over all ratios: BCD 0.389, MCD 0.471. At ratio 0.1: BCD 0.143, MCD 0.152. A kNN-plus-linear-regression conversion method reached FID_inter 1.86 at k = 300. Blending is attributed mainly to specific embedding dimensions.
limits: Image model only, single-word concepts, classifier-based detection. Not a reasoning test.
agent_relevance: A blend is often just co-presence (MCD above BCD): both inputs appear but no fusion. A code check should separate fusion from side-by-side listing.

source: Cho, Zhang, Chen, Inouye (2025) Imagine for me: creative conceptual blending of real images and text via blended attention (IT-Blender)
finding: A diffusion adapter blends a real reference image with a text concept without losing detail. Encoder-only baselines let one concept dominate and fail to disentangle image from text.
numbers: Stable Diffusion test: 200 samples per prompt, 30 prompts, 6,000 samples per baseline. FLUX test: 200 unseen samples x 20 prompts, 4,000 per baseline. In FLUX it had the best visual set consistency and second-best textual consistency. Baselines: IP-Adapter, BLIP-Diffusion, StyleAligned (SD); IP-Adapter, OminiControl, UNO (FLUX).
limits: Automatic metrics (CLIP-based consistency, a ChatGPT blending score in an appendix). The user study mentioned is from other work, not run here.
agent_relevance: Failure to disentangle inputs (one dominates) is the general blending failure mode; our selective-projection step should check that both inputs contribute.

source: Sato (2025) The way we prompt: conceptual blending, neural dynamics, and prompt-induced transitions in LLMs
finding: A conceptual and speculative paper that reads two prompt effects (prompt-induced transition and prompt-induced hallucination) as blending. It reports no controlled results in the text read.
numbers: No sample sizes or effect sizes found. Claims of repeatability across models and sessions rest on the author's earlier preprints.
limits: Low evidential value; single author; no baseline, no blind scoring, no measured effect.
agent_relevance: Do not cite as evidence. Only a hint that fusing very distant domains (for example the periodic table with a poem) invites ungrounded output, which again points to a check.

source: McCaig, DiPaola, Gabora (2016) Deep convolutional networks as models of generalization and blending within visual creativity
finding: Deep Dream and Deep Style are described as visual blending in convolutional networks: one image guides another through chosen layers. The paper relates them to blending theory and honing theory.
numbers: No quantitative evaluation. Descriptive and schematic.
limits: Older and descriptive. Layer choice sets how abstract the blend is, shown by examples only.
agent_relevance: Historical context only: neural blending without a symbolic generic space.

source: Gomez-Ramirez, Herrera-Jaramillo, Geismann (2021) Artificial cognitively-inspired generation of the notion of topological group
finding: A symbolic blending system for mathematics: input theories written in CASL, blend as a colimit of a V-shaped diagram with a generic base, run in the Heterogeneous Tool Set (HETS). Three specifications gave the notion of a topological group.
numbers: Three generated specifications from continuous functions and groups; the paper states the conceptual computations were run and proved in HETS. No error rates.
limits: Only the abstract, introduction and a few passages were read closely. A worked example, not an evaluation. Built on COINVENT-style tooling.
agent_relevance: A code-checkable blend: a blend is accepted only if a prover or consistency check passes. Hard to port to open-text tasks, but shows the pattern of verifying the blend by running it.

source: Song et al. (2025) Is a peeled apple still red? Evaluating LLMs' ability for conceptual combination
url: not located (cited in Schapiro et al. 2026)
finding: Cited by Schapiro et al. as a smaller-scale study that evaluates or proposes ways to improve LLM conceptual combination/blending. Only the citation was read, not the paper.
numbers: Not read; no numbers recorded.
limits: Not opened. Lead only.
agent_relevance: Fetch next to see whether any scaffold improved combination accuracy.

source: Lieto and Pozzato (2018/2020) A description logic framework for commonsense conceptual combination integrating typicality, probabilities and cognitive heuristics (TCL)
finding: Seen only as a title in an arXiv listing: a typicality-based logic system for combining concepts (head and modifier), also used for creative generation. Sibling file evidence_a covers it after reading.
numbers: Not read in this pass.
limits: Title only in this angle's session.
agent_relevance: See evidence_a (a13 to a15) for details; not duplicated here.

source: Cross-study contrast: Wang 2023 and Schapiro 2026 on LLM blending ability
finding: The two results are consistent but concern different steps. PopBlends: ask GPT-3 for bridges, about 56% valid, 93% of pairs have at least one good bridge in five. KOMBINE: only 43.4% of single attempts give a valid generic space across 35 models. Both say: generate several, check each, keep the valid ones.
numbers: 56.7% valid per bridge (GPT-3, 2021) vs 43.4% valid per blend (35 models, 2026). Best-of-five success 93.3% vs not reported.
limits: Different tasks, judges and scoring rules, so the percentages are not directly comparable.
agent_relevance: Argues for generate-many-then-filter with a code check at the generic-space step. It does not show newer models are better at it.

source: Cross-study: scaffolds that improved blending outputs, by size of gain
finding: Across opened studies, the scaffolds that worked all add a named middle step and a check: an explanation or shared-attribute step (IEI), a generic-space-invariant transfer plus diagnostic backtracking, or a bridge-then-expand pipeline. None tested a text-only reasoning task.
numbers: IEI: Midjourney rank 2.40 to 1.98 and win rate 0.26 to 0.35. Schema pipeline: MI 2.75 (plain) to 3.69 (one strong prompt) to 4.56 (full loop). PopBlends tool: 0.87 to 2.03 ideas per pair.
limits: All measure creative image or idea output, judged by people or models. No opened study measures correctness of an answer improved by blending.
agent_relevance: The gap to fill: no published test found that blending improves reasoning accuracy. Our own A/B on a task with ground truth is the missing evidence.

source: Gap statement: LLM agent loops that call a blend operator
finding: The only agent loop found that implements the blending steps as separate agents with a critic is the visual metaphor transfer pipeline; PopBlends is a fixed two-stage pipeline; Misty uses one model call per operation. No search in this session located a blending operator inside a general reasoning or code agent loop.
numbers: Not applicable: absence-of-evidence note. Web search quota was exhausted; only rate-limited arXiv keyword queries on title and abstract were possible.
limits: Search could miss work under other names such as analogy, concept combination, idea recombination.
agent_relevance: Treat our blend operator as untested territory. Plan a controlled test before relying on it.
